summary_html: Agency makes a **substantiated (founded)** finding of abuse/neglect. This decision often unlocks **court petitions**, **service mandates**, and **federal reporting** duties. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)). If a report is marked **indicated**, the full § 26-14-7.1 hearing (counsel, witnesses, cross-examination, subpoenas, an impartial hearing officer) is available only to a person connected with a facility, agency, or home that cares for and controls children; everyone else, including a parent investigated at home, receives the DHR administrative record review, which DHR describes as "provided for those persons not entitled to a hearing" and for which the DHR review page states no deadline (dhr.alabama.gov/child-protective-services/child-abuse-neglect-administrative-reviews).

key_cases.holding: The Court denied State-agent immunity to the CA/N investigator, who never made the home visit required by Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-34-.05(1)(b), and to the ongoing worker, who ignored her supervisor's binding written instructions, but granted immunity to the two supervisors whose duties involved judgment.
key_cases.relevance: The plaintiff challenged the worker's entry of an indicated disposition where unable to complete was the accurate one.
key_cases.quote: because Watson has not submitted substantial evidence indicating that she complied with subsection (b), Watson has not demonstrated that she is entitled to State-agent immunity

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court denied mandamus and upheld a protective order that, after in camera review, limited a parent's discovery of DHR child-abuse records in a dependency case to the names and information of expected witnesses, finding no abuse of discretion.
key_cases.relevance: A parent contesting a finding gets only records relevant and essential to the defense, after in camera review.
key_cases.quote: while this court has the authority to require a judge to exercise proper discretion, we cannot dictate the exercise of that discretion absent a showing of abuse

key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dependency judgments but held that Ala. Code 26-14-8(b)(8), which permits otherwise confidential child-abuse reports to be used by an attorney representing a child or a parent, applies equally in dependency cases as a matter of due process when the information is relevant at the adjudicatory phase, and that refusing to disclose informant names here was error but harmless because no relevancy was shown.
key_cases.relevance: This is the rule Alabama parents actually rely on to see the CA/N reports behind a finding: counsel may use the confidential record when it is relevant at adjudication.
key_cases.quote: We consider it equally applicable to child dependency cases because it represents nothing more than due process when it is relevant information in the adjudicatory phase of the proceedings.

key_cases.case_name: Payne v. State Department of Human Resources
key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a CHINS adjudication initiated by a school superintendent, holding that the juvenile court abused its discretion by denying a continuance where the child's guardian ad litem was given only forty-five minutes to examine the school records that were the sole evidence, defeating the statutory opportunity to examine and controvert written reports under Ala. Code 12-15-65(f).
key_cases.relevance: The opinion states what a family is owed before school or agency records can be used to support a finding against a child: notice and a real opportunity to examine and controvert them.
key_cases.quote: Because a reasonable opportunity was not allowed for preparation of the defense of the accused in this case, we find the court to have abused its judicial discretion.
